transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-11-17 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~47 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Ridgeway Head of AI), Omar Haddad (Platform), Lena Fischer (Security), Tom Becker (SRE)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20281117-ridgeway-54321 (internal note)

Auto-summary (auto): customer needs tight p95 SLOs for short chat and high token/sec streaming for multi-turn workflows. Focus on benchmarking, quantization tradeoffs and private deployment constraints.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off. I'm Maya from Redwood, with Diego our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Priya: Hi all, thanks, I'll hand over to Omar to give a quick overview of what we're trying to solve.
[00:17] Omar: Sure, so Ridgeway is building an operator-facing assistant, lots of short prompts for routing and triage and some longer multi-turn dialogs. Our current goal is p95 under 300ms for the short path and we also need to be able to stream 500-800 tokens/sec in bursts for the multi-turn case. We're evaluating if hosted is enough or we need Dedicated or Private.
[00:42] Diego: Cool. When you say short path under 300ms is that end-to-end on your client, or just server-side generation latency?
[00:50] Tom: Primarily server-side, because our UI adds ~50ms. So if you say server p95 300ms we expect end-to-end around 350ms.
[01:05] Maya: Good, that's helpful. Can you tell us about expected concurrency? How many simultaneous users hitting short prompts?
[01:13] Priya: At peak during a shift change we could see 1k concurrent short requests, sustained over 2-3 minutes, plus background batch jobs. So throughput matters.
[01:24] Diego: OK 1k concurrency for short requests — that shapes sizing a lot. For streaming, are you talking about many concurrent long streams or fewer heavier streams?
[01:33] Priya: A lot fewer, maybe 80-150 concurrent long streams. The short path is the big volume.
[01:40] Diego: Great. A couple clarifying Qs — what models are you evaluating? Open weights or proprietary?
[01:48] Omar: We're starting with an open LLM (we've tried mixed: Llama derivatives), but we might need to move to a more robust variant. Quality drop with quantization is a concern — we want to test int8 and int4 where possible.
[02:02] Diego: Understood. Quantization tradeoffs are model-dependent — some models degrade noticeably at int4 for instruction-following. Our Optimize tool can recommend quantization profiles per-workload.
[02:14] Priya: Can you explain how Redwood routes between Hosted and Dedicated? We heard about automatic fallback if Dedicated saturated.
[02:21] Maya: Sure — you can pin traffic to Dedicated but set routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, or regional. If a Dedicated pool is saturated we can fall back to a compatible hosted variant or a smaller model family automatically, preserving availability. That said fallback does impact latency and sometimes output style.
[02:40] Lena: From security we need to know about KMS, VPC, and audit logs — if we go Dedicated with VPC peering or Private, what's the KMS story?
[02:50] Maya: For Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK) and audit logs for all token-level activity. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer's HSM/KMS and keep control plane in their VPC. We have SOC 2 Type II reports; I'll attach those.
[03:08] Lena: Good. Also need SSO/SAML and RBAC.
[03:12] Maya: Yep, SSO and fine-grained RBAC are supported.
[03:18] Tom: Back to latency — how do you measure p95? Some vendors report only generation time, some include queueing.
[03:26] Diego: We report token generation time plus queueing and network inside our managed path. For Dedicated, you can instrument on-prem agents too. Our Console breaks down queue vs inference vs network at token granularity.
[03:40] Priya: Can you describe the benchmarking approach — we want something reproducible.
[03:45] Diego: We usually provide a perf template: synthetic workload generator that can replay prompts at your target concurrency and sequence length distribution, plus a token-profiler for burst token/sec. We'll also recommend sequences: short prompts ~16-32 tokens, medium ~128 tokens, long streams up to 800 tokens.
[04:03] Priya: Ok that's useful. Can you run an initial benchmark for us or we run it?
[04:07] Maya: We can do both — run a Redwood-hosted benchmark against our Dedicated trial pool we provision for you, and you can run it in your VPC for private testing. The trial Dedicated pool is a short-lived reserved capacity for 2 weeks that we can configure.
[04:22] Omar: Pricing for that trial? Any cost surprises when we scale?
[04:27] Maya: Trial is metered but we give credits for the first two weeks; beyond that it's standard reserved pricing. I'll send a pricing attachment.
[04:36] Priya: About quantization, Diego you said some models suffer at int4. Can you give examples or numbers?
[04:42] Diego: Sure, for instruction-following benchmarks we've seen BLEU/ROUGE-ish drops and hallucination upticks at int4 for certain Llama-family forks. But with fine-tuned instruction models and per-layer calibration the drop can be manageable. We recommend A/B tests on your prompts. Our Optimize tooling suggests per-endpoint profiles: int8 for most cases, int4 for read-only closed-domain with high tolerances.
[05:05] Tom: For the short path are there batching or KV cache tricks to hit the 300ms p95?
[05:11] Diego: Yes — continuous batching and prefix/KV caching are big wins. For very short prompts, you want minimal batching to avoid added latency, but for throughput you can use concurrent micro-batching to improve GPU utilization without hurting p95 too much. KV cache helps multi-turn by avoiding recomputation.
[05:29] Priya: Our prompts are mostly ephemeral, short, and sometimes include a 1-2 sentence context. So caching might help for repeated templates but less so for unique prompts.
[05:39] Diego: Understood. Then sizing will lean toward lower-latency instances and more concurrency headroom.
[05:45] [06:00] (cross talk as someone drops a link)
[06:10] Priya: Another constraint — data residency. Some clients require EU-only. Can Redwood Dedicated be region-locked?
[06:18] Maya: Yes, you can pin Dedicated pools to regions and our Private offering supports full on-prem or VPC setups for strict residency.
[06:26] Lena: For audit logs we need immutable retention for 1 year, can you accommodate?
[06:31] Maya: We have configurable log retention and can integrate with your SIEM for immutable storage. I'll bring the details in the doc pack.
[06:40] Tom: Let's talk rough sizing — if we need 1k short concurrent requests with p95 300ms, any ballpark for GPU footprint?
[06:49] Diego: Ballpark depends on chosen model and sequence length. For a moderately sized model (7-13B equivalent optimized), continuous batching and inference optimizations could deliver ~2000 reqs/sec on a multi-GPU pool, but p95 targets require more headroom. I'd estimate for reliability you'd want a Dedicated cluster equivalent of 8-12 A100-class GPUs for steady 1k concurrency with low p95, but we'll run a benchmark to refine.
[07:16] Priya: That seems reasonable. How do you handle sudden spikes — pre-warm or burst capacity?
[07:22] Maya: Dedicated can be configured with autoscale policies and burst capacity into hosted pools. You can also set canary/fallback rules so if a Dedicated pool can't serve a request within X ms we failover to a hosted variant.
[07:35] Omar: Any throttling behavior we should watch for? We want predictable errors rather than tail latency.
[07:41] Diego: We provide circuit-breakers and rate-limiting at the token and request level, and you can tune behavior to return 429 vs degraded model vs queued.
[07:52] Priya: On model fidelity with quantization — how do you propose we validate quality? Automated evals? Human annotation?
[07:58] Diego: Both. We recommend an eval harness: run your production prompt set through the quantized variant and compare metrics and a human sample for subjective checks. Our platform ties regressions to prompt sets and warns when quality drops exceed thresholds.
[08:14] [08:20] Priya: Great. Let's get specific on the benchmark steps.
[08:23] Diego: Step 1: customer shares top 500 short prompts and 50 long-session transcripts. Step 2: we provide our perf template and recommended concurrency/sequence scripts. Step 3: run targeted runs on Dedicated trial and on hosted and compare p95, tail latency and token/sec. Step 4: if quantization is in play, run same tests with int8/int4 builds.
[08:44] Priya: We'll do step 1 this week.
[08:48] Maya: We'll provision the trial Dedicated pool by next week pending approvals.
[08:52] Omar: What about observability — how granular are the logs? We need per-token cost and latency breakdown by route.
[08:59] Diego: The Console exposes token-level latency breakdowns, per-request traces, and tooling to export to Datadog/Prometheus. We also give token-level cost metrics.
[09:12] Priya: Ok good. Any known gotchas when porting existing prompt templates?
[09:18] Diego: Sometimes instruction tuning differences produce style changes; we usually recommend small prefix adjustments and a validation pass. Also watch for batch-size sensitive sampling differences.
[09:30] Tom: For Private/on-prem — what's the deployment footprint?
[09:35] Maya: Private is flexible: we ship a control plane that talks to your managed agents inside your network, or a fully on-prem package. Hardware requirements vary; for typical loads you provide GPU nodes and we supply the runtime container image and orchestrator.
[09:49] Lena: And compliance reviews — do you do pen tests or provide SOC artifacts?
[09:54] Maya: We can provide reports and are open to joint assessments; for Private deployments we can support customer-led pentests on the infra we supply.
[10:05] Priya: Let's talk SLA — if we go Dedicated what's the p95 SLA?
[10:10] Maya: Our Dedicated SLAs are for uptime and latency envelopes; we can discuss a p95 latency SLO in the contract if there's predictable traffic and pinned capacity. Typically we guarantee availability and commit to performance tiers for certain instance types.
[10:25] Priya: Good. Any examples of customers hitting similar p95?
[10:29] Maya: We have logistics and fleet customers in beta with p95 sub-300ms on short prompts using Dedicated and aggressive batching/caching, we can share anonymized benchmarks.
[10:39] Omar: Back to quantization — what testing time do you need to validate int4 on our prompt set?
[10:45] Diego: If you share prompts now, we can run an automated pass in 48 hours for int8 and int4 and produce a quality delta report within 72 hours.
[10:54] Priya: That's fast, ok.
[10:57] [11:10] (brief silence, people reviewing notes)
[11:20] Tom: For the trial cluster will you expose metrics endpoints to our SREs?
[11:24] Maya: Yes — we'll give read-only access to the Console and optional metrics endpoints that you can pull into your monitoring.
[11:32] Priya: What about cost modeling — tokens vs GPU-hours?
[11:36] Diego: Hosted is token-centric billing, Dedicated is reserved capacity plus usage tiers. We provide a cost modeling tool that converts your token/sec and model choices into monthly GPU-hours and cost estimates. We'll run your numbers in the template.
[11:50] Priya: Any recommended model families that balance latency and quality?
[11:55] Diego: For short p95 goals, optimized 7-13B variants often hit the sweet spot. For high-fidelity responses you might need 70B+ but that's more costly and higher latency. Quantized 13B with int8 often gives good economics.
[12:10] Priya: Ok. Security final Q — is there an option to redact or avoid logging PII?
[12:15] Lena: We need that.
[12:17] Diego: We support token-level redaction and can disable retention for particular endpoints; plus redactors that mask PII before storing logs.
[12:26] [12:40] Maya: Great — sounds like action items: we'll send the perf template, SOC2/KMS docs, and provisioning steps for trial Dedicated. Diego will run initial quantization checks once you share prompts.
[12:54] Priya: Timeline: we aim to decide in 3 weeks pending benchmark results and legal.
[13:02] Maya: Works for us. Any other questions?
[13:06] Tom: Not from SRE.
[13:08] Lena: I'll follow up with security checklist.
[13:11] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[13:14] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the deep dive.
[13:20] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-attributions and minor word errors (e.g., model names misrecognized). References/links shared: perf template link (internal), SOC2 doc link (internal), pricing sheet link (internal).
